title: Krishna's secret naming
hookLine: a sage names a baby in a cowshed, in secret, and calls him the dark one: Kṛṣṇa
carry: namakarana: a name is a family's first blessing
tomorrow: which letters carry an extra breath?

cards: In Gokula, among the cowherds, a baby is growing up who isn't safe. King Kamsa wants him dead. Then Garga, the family priest of the Yadus, arrives at the house of Nanda, the boy's foster father.
Nanda asks him to perform the naming. Garga hesitates. If word gets out, Kamsa will guess who this child really is.
So Nanda says: do it quietly, in the cowshed. No one will know.

teach.b: So in the cowshed, Garga names two boys. The older he calls Rama, for the joy he gives, and Bala, for his strength: Balarama. Then he looks at the dark little one.
In the Bhagavata Purana he says, in paraphrase: in other ages this child came white, red and yellow.

teach.h: NOW HE HAS COME DARK: KṚṢṆA.
teach.b: Now he has come dark. Kṛṣṇa. The name means dark, like a rain cloud.
The ceremony is real, and Hindu families still do it. It's called namakarana, the naming, one of the samskaras, the rites that mark a life.
Often in the first weeks, a priest is called, the name is whispered in the baby's right ear, and the family gives its first blessing.
Many ask which star the baby was born under, since each birth star has starting sounds for a name.
In this tradition a name isn't a label. It's a blessing said again every time someone calls you. Now read the name the careful way: K, r with a dot under it, s with a dot, n with a dot, a.
Kṛṣṇa. Those dots belong to the roof of the mouth.

teach.h: THE DOTS: THE TONGUE CURLS BACK.
teach.b: Curl the tongue back and say ṭa, then ṇa: deeper, almost hollow. The s with a dot is a curled-back sh, as in Viṣṇu. And the r with a dot is a vowel of its own, ṛ.
Some reciters say it close to ri, which gives us the spelling Krishna; others say it closer to ru.
And the week: a palm that says do not fear, a dance offered, work as worship, a name repeated, a sound kept with care, and now a name given.

how: Hindu families mark a baby's naming with namakarana, one of the samskaras: often in the first weeks, a priest is called, the name is whispered in the baby's right ear, and many take the first syllable from the birth star. Students of Sanskrit learn the retroflex sounds and the vowel ṛ in names like Kṛṣṇa.

a strongly trilled r, said like a drum roll

Nanda asked him to do it quietly, in the cowshed, so Kamsa wouldn't guess.
Garga said the child had come in other colors in other ages, and now came dark.
the r with a dot under it in Kṛṣṇa is a vowel
ṛ is a vowel; some say it near ri, others near ru.

games.q: a coworker asks why her Hindu neighbors held a whole ceremony just to name a baby. what fits?
o: namakarana is a samskara: the name is given as the baby's first blessing.
it's only a party; the name was already on the birth certificate.
it's done so the baby is allowed into a temple.
games.why: namakarana is one of the samskaras. even Krishna was given his name this way, by Garga, in secret.

practice: Say ta at the teeth, then curl the tongue back and say ṭa at the roof, back and forth a few times; then na and ṇa the same way. Then say the name slowly, piece by piece: kṛ, ṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa. If you pray, say it as a name, not a word.
If not, say your own name slowly, and think of the first people who said it over you.

wordCard.voice: Ṛ. The r that is a vowel, at the heart of Kṛṣṇa, the name a sage gave in secret, in a cowshed.
